For cross-border work, establish legal responsibility explicitly; the selector does not decide it.

foundations.title: Professional Foundations — British Columbia
foundations.action: Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation.
foundations.record: Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits. Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system. Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions. Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.

care-support.title: Social Care and Support — British Columbia
care-support.action: Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment.
care-support.record: Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception. Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin. Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed. Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.

mca.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia
mca.action: Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test.
mca.record: Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope. Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements. Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework. The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

dols.title: Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia
dols.action: Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections.
dols.record: Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority. Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope. Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review. Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.

mha.title: Mental Health — British Columbia
mha.action: Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives.
mha.record: Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements. Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions. Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route. The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.

safeguarding.title: Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia
safeguarding.action: Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves.
safeguarding.record: Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting. Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed. Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan. Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.

children.title: Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia
children.action: Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold.
children.record: Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger. Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken. Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure. Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.

rights.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia
rights.action: Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation.
rights.record: Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports. Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure. Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route. The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.

sources.title: British Columbia Source Library
sources.action: Check territorial scope, current version, commencement and the relevant service procedure.
sources.record: Record the exact source and provision used, date accessed and any unresolved question.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation. Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits. Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system. Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming every social-work role has identical registration requirements or investigative powers.

flashcardDecks.title: Social Care and Support — British Columbia

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment. Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception. Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin. Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Applying general eligibility criteria without checking exceptions or treating an assessment as guaranteed service delivery.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test. Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope. Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements. Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using the temporary substitute list without checking an existing representative, or treating an agreement as unlimited authority.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act includes limited protective and emergency powers for designated agencies in defined circumstances. Those powers are not a general standing authority for a provider to confine an adult. The least intrusive response and the person’s wishes remain central to the assessment.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections. Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority. Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope. Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating a protection referral or admission consent as authority for ongoing confinement.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The statutory framework includes treatment authority for detained patients, which differs from ordinary substitute-consent healthcare. Do not import another province’s treatment-consent rule. The person’s status, required certificates and the particular treatment must all be checked.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives. Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements. Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions. Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Reducing certification to immediate dangerousness alone or importing another province’s consent rules.

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Designated agencies include regional health bodies and, within defined remits, CLBC and Providence Health Care. The Public Guardian and Trustee has different functions. An adult need not already be a service user for a relevant concern to be considered.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves. Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting. Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed. Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Treating decisional incapability as the only reason an adult may qualify for assistance.

flashcardDecks.title: Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: The Child, Family and Community Service Act (CFCSA) defines a child as a person under 19 and creates a duty to report where its protection conditions are engaged. Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: Indigenous child and family service laws may apply, with provincial guidance explaining referral to an Indigenous authority where relevant. Establish the child’s legal and service context rather than assuming the provincial process is the only possible authority.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold. Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger. Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken. Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Using another province’s reporting age or assuming that every Indigenous child’s case follows an identical provincial route.

flashcardDecks.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia

cards.prompt: Which local framework anchors this topic in British Columbia practice guide?
cards.answer: The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.

cards.prompt: Which distinction must be kept clear?
cards.answer: The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) generally concerns public bodies, while the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) governs covered private organisations. Determine the organisation’s legal status and the information involved before applying collection, disclosure or access rules.

cards.prompt: What are the key local actions?
cards.answer: Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation. Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports. Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure. Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route.

cards.prompt: How can the person participate or challenge the decision?
cards.answer: The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.

cards.prompt: What common error should you avoid?
cards.answer: Assuming public-body and private-organisation privacy rules are interchangeable.

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

glossaryTerms.term: British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW)
glossaryTerms.definition: The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.
Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.
Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.
Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.
Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.
The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.
Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.
Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.
A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.
Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.
Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.
Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.
Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.
Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.
A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.
Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.
Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.
An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.
A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.
An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

theoryLenses.title: Ecological Systems Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.
test: What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

theoryLenses.title: Strengths-Based Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.
test: What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

theoryLenses.title: Trauma-Informed Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.
test: What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

theoryLenses.title: Attachment Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.
test: How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

theoryLenses.title: Systems and Family Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.
test: Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

theoryLenses.title: Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.
test: What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

theoryLenses.title: Crisis Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.
test: What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

theoryLenses.title: Life Course Theory
theoryLenses.focus: Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.
test: What transitions or losses are happening now?
How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

theoryLenses.title: Task-Centred Practice
theoryLenses.focus: Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.
theoryLenses.hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.
test: What problem does the person most want to work on first?
What is the smallest useful next step?
Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

hypothesisSignals.label: Self-neglect, hoarding, home conditions, or repeated crisis presentations.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Think about trauma, executive functioning, environment, identity, isolation, loss, and safeguarding thresholds.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person appears to refuse support, miss visits, or disengage.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Avoid jumping straight to non-compliance. Consider trust, trauma, power, communication, and whether the offer fits the person.

hypothesisSignals.label: Family conflict, carer strain, coercion, or unclear roles are present.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Map roles, power, risk, protective factors, and what happens when professionals intervene.

hypothesisSignals.label: Risk has escalated quickly or a crisis is dominating the assessment.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Separate immediate stabilisation from longer-term formulation and legal route decisions.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is a transition: adolescence to adulthood, hospital discharge, bereavement, moving home, or ageing.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Transitions can disrupt identity, support, eligibility, relationships, and coping.

hypothesisSignals.label: Discrimination, poverty, inaccessible services, stigma, or cultural misunderstanding may be relevant.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Test whether systems are creating or worsening the difficulty.

hypothesisSignals.label: The person or carer feels overwhelmed and cannot see a way forward.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Consider crisis, small steps, stabilisation, advocacy, and practical environmental change.

hypothesisSignals.label: There is mistrust of professionals, fear of services, or repeated complaints.
hypothesisSignals.detail: Explore previous experiences, power, communication, consistency, and whether the person has reason to feel unsafe.

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Safety
childPracticeModels.use: Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What are we worried about, what is working well, and what needs to happen for the child to be safe enough?
test: Can worries be written in plain language that the family understands?
What existing safety has been demonstrated, not just promised?
Who is in the family network and what role can they safely take?

childPracticeModels.title: Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging
childPracticeModels.use: Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.
childPracticeModels.prompt: What would wellbeing, safety, permanence, connection, and belonging look like from the child's perspective?
test: What does the child say or show about where they feel safe and connected?
What would meaningful stability look like in daily life?
How are family relationships, identity, culture, and belonging being protected?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety may improve when adult needs and risks are addressed alongside direct work with the child and family network.
test: Which adult needs are directly affecting child safety or care?
Is the plan joined up across children's and adults' services?
Are adult-focused interventions linked to measurable child safety outcomes?

childPracticeModels.title: Contextual Safeguarding
childPracticeModels.use: Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Harm may be located outside the home, in peer, school, community, or online contexts that parents cannot control alone.
test: Where is harm happening: home, school, peer group, community, online, or transport?
Which context needs intervention, not only which child or parent?
Who has power or influence in that context?

childPracticeModels.title: Family Group Conferencing
childPracticeModels.use: Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The wider family network may hold safe, practical solutions that have not yet been fully mapped or invited in.
test: Who does the child identify as family or trusted network?
What information does the family need before private planning?
How will the plan be checked for safety, clarity, and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Systemic Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The concern may be maintained by family patterns, relationship roles, service responses, or repeated cycles.
test: What pattern repeats, and what keeps it going?
How does each person make sense of the problem?
What would change if one part of the system responded differently?

childPracticeModels.title: Motivational Interviewing
childPracticeModels.use: Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The parent or young person may be caught between reasons to change and reasons to keep things as they are.
test: What does the person want to be different?
What are their reasons for change and reasons against change?
Are we arguing for change so hard that the person argues against it?

childPracticeModels.title: Solution-Focused Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Small exceptions or signs of safety may reveal what can be repeated, strengthened, and built into the plan.
test: When is the problem slightly less serious?
What would one point higher on the safety scale look like?
What has the family already done that helped, even briefly?

childPracticeModels.title: PACE and DDP-Informed Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The child may need relational safety through playfulness, acceptance, curiosity, and empathy before they can reflect or change.
test: How does the child's behaviour make sense as communication or protection?
How can adults stay curious without shaming or escalating?
What helps the child experience safety in the relationship?

childPracticeModels.title: Safe and Together
childPracticeModels.use: Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Child safety work should focus on the perpetrator's pattern of behaviour and avoid blaming the non-abusive parent for the abuse.
test: What is the perpetrator's pattern and impact on the child?
What has the protective parent done to promote safety?
Does the plan increase accountability for the person causing harm?

childPracticeModels.title: Graded Care Profile 2
childPracticeModels.use: Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.
childPracticeModels.prompt: The quality of care may need structured, observable mapping rather than vague descriptions of neglect.
test: Which care domains are strong, inconsistent, or harmful?
What evidence has been observed rather than assumed?
Is change measurable across time and review?

childPracticeModels.title: Restorative Practice
childPracticeModels.use: Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.
childPracticeModels.prompt: Progress may come through relationship repair, accountability, and shared planning rather than only professional direction.
test: Who has been affected and what do they need?
What repair or accountability is realistic and safe?
How will the meeting avoid blame and keep the child central?

childModelSignals.label: Child protection concerns, safety planning, or danger statements are needed.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs clear worries, existing safety, safety goals, family network planning, and review.

childModelSignals.label: Neglect, home conditions, missed health needs, or inconsistent care are central.
childModelSignals.detail: The assessment needs observable evidence, care domains, impact on the child, and change over time.

childModelSignals.label: Domestic abuse is affecting the child or family safety.
childModelSignals.detail: The plan needs perpetrator pattern analysis, protective parent strengths, child impact, and safe information sharing.

childModelSignals.label: Exploitation, adolescent risk, peer harm, school risk, or online/community harm is present.
childModelSignals.detail: Risk may sit outside the home and require contextual mapping beyond parent-focused plans.

childModelSignals.label: The child is in care, on the edge of care, returning home, or permanence is uncertain.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs belonging, stability, identity, relationships, family network options, and safe permanence planning.

childModelSignals.label: Trauma, attachment disruption, mistrust, shame, or relational conflict is central.
childModelSignals.detail: The child may need relational safety and adults who can stay curious, calm, boundaried, and empathic.

childModelSignals.label: There may be wider family or trusted network members who could help.
childModelSignals.detail: The network may hold safe options for care, practical support, supervision, or belonging.

childModelSignals.label: A parent or young person feels ambivalent, defensive, stuck, or hard to engage.
childModelSignals.detail: The work needs careful engagement, change talk, respect for autonomy, and clarity about non-negotiable safety.

childModelSignals.label: There has been conflict, harm, school exclusion, relationship breakdown, or a need for repair.
childModelSignals.detail: The work may need accountability, safe dialogue, relationship repair, and a shared plan.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Professional Foundations — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker assumes that employment by a health authority automatically gives them the powers of a designated adult-protection investigator.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the organisation’s designation and the worker’s actual role, authority and procedure. Gather relevant social evidence within scope and arrange the appropriate designated-agency response. Employment and statutory investigative authority should not be conflated.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Social Care and Support — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A recently arrived older adult is told that a general residence requirement means no assessment or alternative support can be considered.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the published exceptions and the person’s actual health needs and circumstances. Identify any other relevant service while the eligibility question is resolved. Record reasons, interim support and the route for challenging the decision.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Decision-Making and Capacity — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A friend offers to consent to treatment because they visit most often, although a valid representation agreement may appoint somebody else.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Assess the adult’s own ability and read the agreement. Determine the appropriate healthcare-consent route and priority before seeking consent. Frequent contact is useful evidence about wishes but does not by itself establish authority.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Restrictions and Liberty — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A care facility locks a resident’s door after an adult-protection referral and says the referral gives it authority to continue indefinitely.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Clarify whether any lawful emergency or court measure exists and its limits. Review the actual restriction and the adult’s wishes, arrange safer alternatives and obtain the appropriate legal or designated-agency advice. A referral itself confers no indefinite detention power.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Mental Health — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person is detained and a worker assumes the treatment-consent process must be identical to the one used in a neighbouring province.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Read the BC provisions governing the person’s actual status and proposed treatment. Explain the specific review and second-opinion rights, and assess unrelated physical healthcare under its own framework. Avoid substituting a familiar out-of-province process.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Adult Safeguarding — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A person understands that a family member is taking money but is physically prevented from leaving home or contacting services.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Consider the inability to seek assistance and the relevant designated-agency route rather than rejecting the concern because the person understands the abuse. Arrange safe communication, practical protection and any police response, with the adult’s wishes clearly recorded.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Children, Families and Transitions — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A worker hears a serious concern about an 18-year-old and dismisses it because the worker previously practised where adult services began earlier.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Check the BC age definition and applicable protection conditions. Make the appropriate report and coordinate support with the young person’s participation. Identify any relevant Indigenous authority and transition arrangements rather than importing the former jurisdiction’s boundary.

scenarioWorkouts.title: Rights, Culture and Recording — British Columbia
scenarioWorkouts.summary: A private community provider copies a public health authority’s privacy form and assumes that the same disclosure powers apply.
prompts: Which local framework and decision-maker apply?
What evidence and support could change the next step?
How will the person participate, challenge and obtain review?
scenarioWorkouts.reveal: Determine the provider’s actual legal obligations and purpose of sharing. Revise the consent and information process to fit the applicable law, and record what the person was told. Similar work does not establish identical statutory powers.

printableTemplates.title: Professional Foundations
printableTemplates.summary: Explain your professional role, distinguish an ethical concern from a statutory power, and turn a formulation into an accountable plan.
printableTemplates.body:
Professional Foundations
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The British Columbia College of Social Workers (BCCSW) Code of Ethics and Standards of Practice and the Social Workers Act provide the professional framework. Check the registration category, scope and any applicable statutory exemption or special role; a job title alone does not explain a practitioner’s regulatory position.

Health authorities, Community Living BC (CLBC), child and family services, Indigenous authorities and community organisations have different remits. Identify the organisation exercising the function and the law governing it. Cultural safety includes attention to Indigenous self-determination, racism and the person’s chosen community relationships.

Local pathway:
Confirm the practitioner’s role, regulatory position and any specific statutory designation.
Explain the purpose of involvement, participation and confidentiality limits.
Map the responsible health, community, child-service or Indigenous authority rather than treating all services as one system.
Use supervision and continuing learning to test evidence, bias and the practical effect of decisions.

Recording prompts:
1. Your role and the legal or professional framework
Notes:

2. The person’s outcomes and communication preferences
Notes:

3. Evidence, competing explanations and missing perspectives
Notes:

4. Power, boundaries and any conflict of interest
Notes:

5. Agreed action, supervision, feedback and review
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Distinguish a BCCSW professional complaint from a health-authority, service, privacy or statutory decision review. Help the person identify which body can address the action or remedy in question.

Sources:
https://bccsw.ca/for-registrants/standards-scope-of-practice/
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/08031_01

printableTemplates.title: Social Care and Support
printableTemplates.summary: Map assessment, eligibility, funding and delivery separately; include family support without assuming it; explain the local route for challenging a decision.
printableTemplates.body:
Social Care and Support
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Publicly subsidised home and community care involves health-authority assessment, general eligibility and service-specific criteria. Provincial guidance addresses status, residence, age and health-related need, with exceptions to some general conditions. Do not convert a general criterion into an absolute exclusion without checking those exceptions.

Home support, long-term care, assisted living, CLBC supports and income assistance are different programmes. Needs assessment, access priority, client contribution and actual provision must be distinguished. The responsible office should explain which programme and policy support the decision.

Local pathway:
Contact the appropriate health-authority home and community care service for eligibility and needs assessment.
Check general and service-specific criteria, including any relevant exception.
Record assessed needs, family willingness, priority, costs and when support will actually begin.
Obtain reasons and the applicable health-authority review or complaint process if access or service levels are disputed.

Recording prompts:
1. Daily-life evidence, fluctuation and desired outcomes
Notes:

2. The service, eligibility test and decision-maker
Notes:

3. Carer willingness and separately identified needs
Notes:

4. Funding, charges, decisions and reasons
Notes:

5. Start dates, unmet needs, contingency and challenge route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Provincial guidance distinguishes complaints about care from appeals of home and community care service decisions. Use the current health-authority process and decision notice. A provider complaint will not necessarily review a funding or eligibility decision.

Sources:
https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/are-you-eligible
https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/how-to-arrange-for-care
https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/accessing-health-care/home-community-care/concerns-and-complaints

printableTemplates.title: Decision-Making and Capacity
printableTemplates.summary: Identify the precise decision, provide practical decision support, apply the local capacity or consent framework and verify a representative’s authority.
printableTemplates.body:
Decision-Making and Capacity
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act has separate health-care and facility-admission provisions. The Representation Agreement Act and Patients Property Act provide other forms of authority. Identify the decision and the relevant document before deciding which route applies. For healthcare, the provider assesses whether the adult understands the relevant treatment information and its application to their own situation. Adapt communication to the adult’s abilities; a communication difference alone does not establish incapability.

Where temporary substitute consent for healthcare is needed, the healthcare provider selects the first available qualified person in the statutory list. The person’s prior capable instructions or wishes and the Act’s decision standard matter. An available relative is not automatically entitled to displace an authorised representative or another person with priority.

Local pathway:
Support the adult’s own decision and apply the relevant statutory incapability test.
Check any advance directive, representation agreement or committee order and its scope.
Where the temporary substitute route applies, use the statutory priority and qualification requirements.
Separate healthcare consent from admission and from personal or financial decisions under another framework.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, options and time at which it is needed
Notes:

2. Communication support and observed responses
Notes:

3. Applicable legal test and evidence for each element
Notes:

4. Representative’s document, scope and decision standard
Notes:

5. Wishes, disagreement, review and any urgent action
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Public Guardian and Trustee has relevant functions when a suitable substitute is unavailable or authority is disputed. Court or other statutory review may be needed depending on the issue. Explain the specific route and preserve the adult’s participation.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96405_01

printableTemplates.title: Restrictions and Liberty
printableTemplates.summary: Describe actual restrictions, identify the setting-specific legal authority, test alternatives and make representation and review practical.
printableTemplates.body:
Restrictions and Liberty
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Care-facility admission consent, treatment consent and authority for restraint or detention are distinct. The Health Care (Consent) and Care Facility (Admission) Act, facility licensing rules and Mental Health Act may apply in different circumstances. Read the actual measure and legal setting rather than treating admission as permission for every restriction.

Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act includes limited protective and emergency powers for designated agencies in defined circumstances. Those powers are not a general standing authority for a provider to confine an adult. The least intrusive response and the person’s wishes remain central to the assessment.

Local pathway:
Describe the restriction, who enforces it and the adult’s wishes or objections.
Identify the applicable facility, mental-health or designated-agency framework and the precise authority.
Check any order, emergency condition, monitoring duty and limit on duration or scope.
Explore alternatives and arrange the relevant independent support, complaint or legal review.

Recording prompts:
1. Each restriction, setting, duration and actual effect
Notes:

2. The person’s wishes, understanding and objections
Notes:

3. Legal authority, decision-maker, limits and conditions
Notes:

4. Alternatives tried and the evidence about necessity
Notes:

5. Representation, review date, expiry and challenge
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Mental-health detention has review-panel and court routes; other disputed restrictions may require different legal advice or service-regulation responses. A healthcare substitute or a family member cannot be assumed to authorise every liberty restriction.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96181_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01

printableTemplates.title: Mental Health
printableTemplates.summary: Distinguish voluntary care, compulsory assessment, detention and treatment; connect the local criteria to evidence and explain the person’s review rights.
printableTemplates.body:
Mental Health
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Mental Health Act provides involuntary admission through medical certification and other defined routes. Section 22 addresses mental disorder requiring treatment, need for treatment in or through a designated facility, need for care, supervision and control to prevent substantial deterioration or protect the person or others, and inability to be suitably admitted voluntarily.

The statutory framework includes treatment authority for detained patients, which differs from ordinary substitute-consent healthcare. Do not import another province’s treatment-consent rule. The person’s status, required certificates and the particular treatment must all be checked.

Local pathway:
Identify the route and evidence for each applicable criterion, including voluntary alternatives.
Check certificates, dates, notices and renewal or review requirements.
Identify the legal basis for psychiatric treatment and distinguish unrelated healthcare decisions.
Arrange rights advice, access to a review panel or court process and the applicable second-opinion route.

Recording prompts:
1. Mental and physical health evidence and the person’s account
Notes:

2. The local criteria and voluntary alternatives considered
Notes:

3. Separate authority for transport, admission and treatment
Notes:

4. Required notices, advocacy, representation and review
Notes:

5. Continuity, discharge responsibilities and crisis plan
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Act includes rights advice, notice, review panels, court discharge applications and a second-medical-opinion provision. These mechanisms address different questions. Explain the route that fits the person’s concern rather than presenting a treatment complaint as identical to detention review.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96288_01

printableTemplates.title: Adult Safeguarding
printableTemplates.summary: Recognise abuse, neglect and coercion; choose the correct local reporting route; connect immediate protection to the adult’s wishes and continuing support.
printableTemplates.body:
Adult Safeguarding
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
Part 3 of the Adult Guardianship Act concerns abuse, neglect or self-neglect where an adult cannot seek support and assistance because of the specified restraint, disability, illness, injury or decision-related conditions. Designated agencies must look into relevant reports. The statutory threshold and agency role should be stated explicitly.

Designated agencies include regional health bodies and, within defined remits, CLBC and Providence Health Care. The Public Guardian and Trustee has different functions. An adult need not already be a service user for a relevant concern to be considered.

Local pathway:
Identify the alleged harm and why the adult may be unable to seek assistance themselves.
Refer to the designated agency appropriate to the person and setting.
Arrange immediate safety and consider police or other statutory duties where needed.
Separate voluntary support, investigation, emergency action and a court-backed support-and-assistance plan.

Recording prompts:
1. Concern, source, chronology and the adult’s own account
Notes:

2. Immediate safety and a safe communication method
Notes:

3. The local reporting threshold, recipient and timing
Notes:

4. Consent, coercion and information-sharing basis
Notes:

5. Accepted responsibilities, outcomes and follow-up
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Preserve the adult’s participation and use the Act’s principles concerning autonomy and effective, least intrusive support. A designated-agency investigation is not the same as appointing a substitute decision-maker. Obtain advice where an imposed plan or emergency power is proposed.

Sources:
https://www.trustee.bc.ca/adults/protecting-vulnerable-adult-abuse-neglect-or-self-neglect
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96006_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/11_19_2002

printableTemplates.title: Children, Families and Transitions
printableTemplates.summary: Separate family support from protection powers, apply the local reporting duty, involve the child and coordinate education, health and transition planning.
printableTemplates.body:
Children, Families and Transitions
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The Child, Family and Community Service Act (CFCSA) defines a child as a person under 19 and creates a duty to report where its protection conditions are engaged. Do not apply another province’s age boundary. A report should reach the appropriate child-protection authority; telling a supervisor alone is insufficient.

Indigenous child and family service laws may apply, with provincial guidance explaining referral to an Indigenous authority where relevant. Establish the child’s legal and service context rather than assuming the provincial process is the only possible authority.

Local pathway:
Identify the concern and the child’s age, using the CFCSA reporting threshold.
Make the report through the appropriate provincial or Indigenous-authority arrangements and address immediate danger.
Record the child’s words, evidence, cultural relationships and actions taken.
Coordinate support and participation while distinguishing a report, investigation, agreement and court measure.

Recording prompts:
1. Child’s account, communication and daily-life evidence
Notes:

2. Harm, strengths, needs and alternative explanations
Notes:

3. Reporting duty, recipient and action taken
Notes:

4. Family participation, culture and legal authority
Notes:

5. Named plan, education/health links and transition dates
Notes:

Challenge and review:
Explain who is responding and how the child and family can obtain advocacy, legal advice or a complaint review. Respect the applicable Indigenous jurisdiction and do not delay an urgent safety report while assuming that another organisation will act.

Sources:
https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/safety/public-safety/protecting-children/reporting-child-abuse
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96046_01

printableTemplates.title: Rights, Culture and Recording
printableTemplates.summary: Connect rights to an actual service decision, distinguish privacy from absolute secrecy and write a record that makes reasons and disagreement visible.
printableTemplates.body:
Rights, Culture and Recording
British Columbia practice guide practice guide
Learning prompt, not an official statutory form. Use fictional or anonymised information.

Local framework:
The BC Human Rights Code applies to discrimination in its covered areas, while the Canadian Charter has a distinct scope. Indigenous rights and applicable Indigenous laws must be considered in the actual function, alongside professional cultural-safety responsibilities.

The Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA) generally concerns public bodies, while the Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) governs covered private organisations. Determine the organisation’s legal status and the information involved before applying collection, disclosure or access rules.

Local pathway:
Identify the service decision, relevant right and responsible organisation.
Consider accommodation, language, cultural safety and the person’s chosen supports.
Check whether FIPPA, PIPA or another specific rule applies to the record and disclosure.
Record the lawful purpose, necessary information, reasons and the access, correction or complaint route.

Recording prompts:
1. Decision, affected rights and responsible organisation
Notes:

2. Accessibility, culture and participation arrangements
Notes:

3. Disclosure purpose, legal basis, recipient and limits
Notes:

4. Evidence, alternatives, reasons and disagreement
Notes:

5. Access, correction, complaints and review route
Notes:

Challenge and review:
The Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner for BC addresses matters within FIPPA and PIPA; the Human Rights Tribunal addresses Code complaints. Professional and service complaints are separate. Help the person select the route that can address their concern.

Sources:
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96210_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/03063_01
https://www.bclaws.gov.bc.ca/civix/document/id/complete/statreg/96165_00
